I am 59 years old and have been farming these lands in Quzhou County my entire life. With the education I have, I pay close attention to what the agricultural extension station recommends, but I also trust my own eyes and experience. Around here, the soil is good alluvial loam, and the climate gives us enough heat and light for two crops a year if we manage water carefully. I do not see any reason to break from the wheat-maize rotation that has reliably fed my family and produced a marketable surplus. The key is doing it well: choosing the right varieties, timing fertilizer to match crop needs, and irrigating at the critical growth stages.

This year I will plant **winter wheat** on all my land in late October and follow it with **summer maize** immediately after the June harvest. I have 8 mu in total. For wheat, I will use an improved semi-dwarf variety that resists lodging and has good resistance to stripe rust, which has been a problem lately. For maize, I will plant a high-yield hybrid with dense planting tolerance. I will apply base fertilizer before sowing and top-dress nitrogen at jointing for wheat, and at the large trumpet stage for maize. I will irrigate wheat four times and maize three times, because rainfall on the North China Plain is unreliable in spring and early summer. I will do rotary tillage before wheat sowing to create a fine seedbed, but after wheat harvest I will minimize tillage for maize to save time and moisture. I will spray pesticides two to three times per crop, mainly for weeds and aphids on wheat, and for corn borer and weeds on maize.
